title: Everyday Fluency Upgrade
description: Connectors, discourse markers, and idiomatic phrases that make your English sound natural and fluid.

words.definitionEn: Although; even though — used to introduce a concession that doesn't change the main point.
words.exampleSentence: The meeting was productive, albeit a little long.
words.nuance: More formal than 'although' but sounds sophisticated in both writing and speech.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'albeit' to soften a mild criticism: 'Good work, albeit with a few gaps.'

words.definitionEn: In spite of that; even so — used to contrast with what was just said.
words.exampleSentence: The data is incomplete. Nevertheless, the trends are clear.
words.nuance: Slightly more formal than 'however' — excellent for pivoting in arguments.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'nevertheless' to acknowledge a counterpoint then restate your position.

words.definitionEn: In addition to what has been said; used to add another supporting point.
words.exampleSentence: The proposal is cost-effective. Furthermore, it aligns with our long-term strategy.
words.nuance: Stronger than 'also' — implies the new point reinforces and extends your argument.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'furthermore' in presentations to build your case point by point.

words.definitionEn: As a result of what has just been described; therefore.
words.exampleSentence: The supplier failed to deliver. Consequently, we had to source an alternative.
words.nuance: More formal than 'so' — shows clear cause-and-effect thinking in speech and writing.
words.realLifeTask: Replace 'so' with 'consequently' in presentations to sound more analytical.

words.definitionEn: In contrast to the fact that; used to highlight a difference between two things.
words.exampleSentence: The UK market is growing steadily, whereas the US market has plateaued.
words.nuance: More precise than 'but' — specifically signals a direct comparison or contrast.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'whereas' when comparing two distinct options or situations in reports.

words.definitionEn: Having a tendency or inclination towards something, often something negative.
words.exampleSentence: The system is prone to errors when the server is under heavy load.
words.nuance: Often used for negative tendencies — 'prone to mistakes', 'prone to overreacting'.
words.realLifeTask: Identify what you're 'prone to' professionally and work to mitigate those tendencies.

words.definitionEn: Certain or very likely to happen.
words.exampleSentence: With this level of demand, prices are bound to rise.
words.nuance: Expresses strong prediction or inevitability — more confident than 'likely to'.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'bound to' to signal confident predictions: 'It's bound to cause confusion.'

words.definitionEn: To give a particular impression or appear to be a certain way to others.
words.exampleSentence: I don't want to come across as dismissive, but I disagree.
words.nuance: Crucial for self-awareness — how you come across may differ from how you intend to be seen.
words.realLifeTask: Ask for feedback: 'Did I come across as too direct in that meeting?'

words.definitionEn: To tolerate or endure something unpleasant without complaining.
words.exampleSentence: She put up with the difficult client for months before escalating.
words.nuance: Implies you're tolerating something you'd prefer to stop — often used with frustration.
words.realLifeTask: Recognise what you've been 'putting up with' — then decide whether to address it or accept it.

words.definitionEn: To do something wrong or questionable and avoid punishment or consequences.
words.exampleSentence: You can't get away with poor quality work in a competitive market.
words.nuance: Implies avoiding fair consequences — useful in both literal and figurative contexts.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'you can't get away with' to signal that standards matter in your team.

words.definitionEn: To compensate for something negative by providing something positive.
words.exampleSentence: The strong Q4 results made up for the slow start to the year.
words.nuance: Implies compensation restores balance — often used when acknowledging earlier shortfalls.
words.realLifeTask: Reassure clients by showing how you'll make up for any delays or issues.

words.definitionEn: To get to the important point without wasting time on preliminaries.
words.exampleSentence: Let me cut to the chase — we need a 20% budget increase.
words.nuance: Direct and assertive — signals you value efficiency; use when time is short.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'let me cut to the chase' to signal urgency and directness in important conversations.

words.definitionEn: Undecided between two options; not committed to either side.
words.exampleSentence: I'm still on the fence about whether to accept the offer.
words.nuance: Neutral — implies you can see merit in both options, not that you're weak.
words.realLifeTask: Be honest in discussions: 'I'm still on the fence — can you help me see the risks more clearly?'

words.definitionEn: To start a new role, project, or activity with energy and immediately be productive.
words.exampleSentence: She hit the ground running and delivered results in her first week.
words.nuance: Positive — implies preparation, confidence, and readiness. Common in job descriptions.
words.realLifeTask: Prepare well for new roles so you can 'hit the ground running' from day one.

translations.pl: zacząć z impetem / od razu do pracy

words.definitionEn: Included in and aware of the current information or communication about something.
words.exampleSentence: Please keep me in the loop on any updates with the client.
words.nuance: Very common in professional settings — signals you expect ongoing communication.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'keep me in the loop' when delegating tasks to maintain oversight.

words.definitionEn: Having the latest information; performing at the expected or required level.
words.exampleSentence: Can you bring the new hire up to speed on our processes?
words.nuance: Common in onboarding contexts — 'get up to speed' = learn what you need to know quickly.
words.realLifeTask: Create onboarding documents to bring new team members up to speed quickly.

words.definitionEn: Not noticed or attracting attention; happening without others being aware.
words.exampleSentence: The problem had been growing under the radar for months before anyone noticed.
words.nuance: Can be positive (intentional discretion) or negative (missed problem) — context clarifies.
words.realLifeTask: Watch for risks 'flying under the radar' in your projects — check assumptions regularly.

words.term: at the end of the day
words.definitionEn: When everything has been considered; ultimately; what matters most.
words.exampleSentence: We can debate the details, but at the end of the day, the results speak for themselves.
synonyms: when all is said and done
words.nuance: Common and versatile — signals you're getting to the essential point, cutting through complexity.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'at the end of the day' to pivot from detail to what truly matters in a discussion.

words.definitionEn: In all practical senses; effectively; as far as practical results are concerned.
words.exampleSentence: The project is, for all intents and purposes, finished.
words.nuance: Signals that the reality matches the description, even if technicalities differ.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'for all intents and purposes' to draw a practical conclusion despite technical nuance.

words.definitionEn: Used to introduce something that is so obvious it shouldn't need stating — yet you're stating it for emphasis.
words.exampleSentence: Needless to say, missing a client deadline has consequences.
words.nuance: Slightly ironic — you're saying something you claim is obvious. Use for emphasis, not condescension.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'needless to say' to emphasise an obvious but important point without over-explaining.

words.definitionEn: Similarly; in the same way; for the same reason — draws a parallel between two things.
words.exampleSentence: If we expect flexibility from our team, by the same token, we must offer it too.
words.nuance: Shows logical consistency — you're applying the same logic to both sides.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'by the same token' when making a reciprocal argument or drawing a parallel.

translations.uk: з тієї ж причини / так само

words.definitionEn: In general terms; as a general statement that may have exceptions.
words.exampleSentence: Broadly speaking, the feedback has been positive.
words.nuance: Signals a generalisation — honest acknowledgement that you're not covering every case.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'broadly speaking' to give general impressions without overstating certainty.

words.definitionEn: If we apply the exact rules or definitions — precisely and technically.
words.exampleSentence: Strictly speaking, this falls outside the scope of the original agreement.
words.nuance: Signals you're applying a strict interpretation — useful when precision matters.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'strictly speaking' when you need to be technically accurate but want to sound measured.

words.definitionEn: When looking back on past events with the benefit of knowing how things turned out.
words.exampleSentence: In retrospect, we should have raised those concerns earlier.
words.nuance: Useful for honest post-mortems and lessons learned — signals reflection, not blame.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'in retrospect' in project reviews to draw honest conclusions without pointing fingers.

words.definitionEn: Understanding something better after it has already happened.
words.exampleSentence: In hindsight, the warning signs were there all along.
words.nuance: Slightly more conversational than 'in retrospect' — both signal reflective thinking.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'in hindsight' to share lessons without implying you should have known better.

words.term: off the top of my head
words.definitionEn: Without thinking carefully or checking — giving an immediate, approximate answer.
words.exampleSentence: Off the top of my head, I'd say the budget is around £50,000.
words.nuance: Signals honesty — you're giving a rough estimate and the listener should verify the detail.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'off the top of my head' to give quick estimates without committing to exact figures.

words.definitionEn: In the current situation or state, without any changes.
words.exampleSentence: As it stands, we won't hit the deadline without additional resources.
words.nuance: Often used to present an honest current picture — implies things may change.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'as it stands' in status updates to give a clear current snapshot.

translations.pl: w obecnym stanie / tak jak jest

words.definitionEn: Taking everything into account — acknowledging complexity before a balanced judgement.
words.exampleSentence: All things considered, I think we made the right call.
synonyms: when all is said and done
words.nuance: Signals a balanced, considered conclusion — implies you've weighed the pros and cons.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'all things considered' to present a nuanced, balanced verdict in discussions.

words.definitionEn: After thinking more carefully about something; having reconsidered.
words.exampleSentence: On reflection, I think we need a different approach.
words.nuance: Shows intellectual humility — you've thought it through and may have changed your view.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'on reflection' to politely revise a position: 'On reflection, I think I was too hasty.'

words.definitionEn: Used to re-explain something in another way for clarity.
words.exampleSentence: The system is inefficient. To put it differently, we're paying twice for half the result.
words.nuance: Useful when your first explanation wasn't clear — rephrase the idea, not just repeat it.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'to put it differently' when you sense your audience hasn't quite understood you.

words.definitionEn: Used when a thought or realisation occurs to you in the middle of conversation.
words.exampleSentence: Come to think of it, we never actually got sign-off on that change.
synonyms: now that I think about it
words.nuance: Sounds natural and spontaneous — great for simulating thinking in real time in conversation.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'come to think of it' to introduce a newly occurring thought naturally in meetings.

words.definitionEn: Keeping the previously mentioned point in consideration; given what has just been said.
words.exampleSentence: Costs are rising. With that in mind, we should review the pricing model.
words.nuance: Creates a logical bridge — 'here's the context, so here's what we should do about it'.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'with that in mind' to connect context to recommendation in presentations.

words.definitionEn: Despite what has just been stated; introducing a contrasting or qualifying point.
words.exampleSentence: The results are encouraging. That being said, there are still risks to manage.
words.nuance: Smooth pivot between agreeing with a point and introducing a qualification.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'that being said' to acknowledge the positive before introducing a caveat.

words.definitionEn: Used to introduce an opinion or piece of information that may or may not be valuable.
words.exampleSentence: For what it's worth, I think the original plan was stronger.
words.nuance: Expresses gentle humility — you're sharing a view but not insisting it be acted upon.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'for what it's worth' to offer opinions diplomatically without being pushy.

words.definitionEn: To remember or consider a particular fact or point when making decisions.
words.exampleSentence: Bear in mind that the figures are estimates, not confirmed data.
words.nuance: Useful for flagging caveats and important context — reminds the listener of something.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'bear in mind' to flag assumptions or limitations in your recommendations.

words.definitionEn: To consider a factor or detail when making a decision or judgement.
words.exampleSentence: We need to take the regulatory changes into account before finalising the strategy.
words.nuance: Implies thoroughness — taking multiple factors into account leads to better decisions.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'take into account' in written proposals to show comprehensive thinking.

words.definitionEn: To highlight the difference between two things that might be confused.
words.exampleSentence: I want to draw a distinction between feedback and criticism.
words.nuance: Signals analytical clarity — useful when two concepts are often confused.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'I want to draw a distinction' to clarify nuanced differences in presentations.

words.definitionEn: On the whole; in general; considering all aspects.
words.exampleSentence: By and large, the rollout has gone smoothly.
words.nuance: Slightly informal but widely used — a natural alternative to 'generally speaking'.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'by and large' in conversational updates: 'By and large, the team is on board.'

words.term: in the grand scheme of things
words.definitionEn: When viewed in the context of the bigger picture or overall situation.
words.exampleSentence: The delay is frustrating, but in the grand scheme of things, it won't affect the outcome.
words.nuance: Useful for providing perspective and reducing catastrophising in tense situations.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'in the grand scheme of things' to offer perspective when a team member is stressed about minor setbacks.

translations.uk: в загальній перспективі / якщо дивитися ширше
translations.pl: w szerszym kontekście / w wielkim rozrachunku
translations.ru: в общей перспективе / если смотреть шире
